extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and advanced law students (practitioners of U.S. patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and procedural rules governing patent reissues and extensions in U.S. law: timeliness, identity ("same invention"), surrender effects, who may apply, scope/no-new-matter limits, evidentiary presumptions, and effect of reissued or extended patents. Targets practitioners deciding or litigating reissue/extension applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness for broadened reissue (delay rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: General rule: a delay for two years or more invalidates a broadened reissue unless that delay is accounted for and excused by special circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts exercise liberality in favor of patentees in borderline cases, but long delays (examples: 13–15 years) have been excused in some cases while much shorter delays have been held fatal in others (even 97 days when adverse rights intervened). Receiving erroneous advice from patent counsel is not an excuse for waiting a long time. In a plain case, less than two years can still defeat a broadened reissue; six months is probably the maximum ordinarily excusable, though peculiar facts have excused seven months. A decision on double patenting (two patents for same invention) makes it urgent to seek reissue promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two‑year public‑use/on‑sale bar does not apply to reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory provision that makes a patent void if the invention was in public use or on sale more than two years before application does not apply to reissue patents and their applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reissue application is considered appended to the original application, and the two‑year period ceases to run with the filing of the reissue; novelty for the reissue still dates from the original invention/filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender need not be written (parol surrender)
rubrics_metrics.description: A surrender of a patent when made with an application for a reissue need not be made in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reissue stating it is a reissue of a surrendered former reissue is not negatived by production of a document purporting to be a written surrender. There is a presumption that the proper patent was surrendered (including by parol), and an ineffectual written attempt to surrender does not rebut that presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of surrender depending on date (pre/post July 8, 1870)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents surrendered prior to July 8, 1870 were canceled in law whether a reissue was granted or not; patents surrendered since July 8, 1870 were canceled thereby if reissues were granted, but not otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A surrendered patent cannot be enforced while an application for a reissue is pending. If a reissue application is rejected or withdrawn, the original patent stands unaffected by what occurred while the reissue application was pending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery for infringement of a surrendered patent (damages/profits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily no damages or profits can be recovered for infringement of a surrendered patent committed prior to its cancellation by means of any judgment entered after that cancellation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Money recovered or voluntarily paid on account of such infringement prior to cancellation cannot be recovered back. Exception exists where the defendant infringer was himself the patentee and held patents in trust for equitable grantees — in such equitable circumstances the infringer may be required to account for profits despite surrender and reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissuing a reissued patent and final expiration bar
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissued patent may be surrendered and reissued again under the same circumstances as an original patent reissue, and the last reissue may be identical with the original patent; but no reissue can be granted after the patent's final expiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prohibition applies even where a foreign patent expired and the U.S. patent sought to be reissued does not on its face show expiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Same invention' requirement for reissue (Parker & Whipple rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only 'the same invention' can be covered by a reissued patent; the Supreme Court defined this as whatever invention was described in the original letters patent and appears therein to have been intended to be secured thereby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This meaning excludes basing a reissue claim solely on a model or drawing or on materials not appearing in the original letters patent as intended to be secured. Models, drawings, and descriptions cannot alone support a reissue claim unless the original letters patent's description shows the invention was intended to be secured originally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner proof clause (when no model or drawing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is neither model nor drawing, amendments may be made upon proof, satisfactory to the Commissioner, that such new matter or amendment was part of the original invention and was omitted from the specification by inadvertence, accident, or mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The clause does not enlarge the Commissioner's power regarding what invention may be reissued; its meaning is limited and not fully expansive.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'No new matter' provision (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory provision that 'no new matter shall be introduced into the specification' is another way of saying a reissued patent shall be for the same invention as the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision does not prevent stating a new use of an invention shown in the original, explaining operation in a reissue when only described originally, or varying the description of something described in the original — such additions are not considered 'new matter' in this sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissued patents must compare to surrendered reissues as well as original
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissued patents granted on the surrender of former reissues must endure comparison, on identity of invention, with the original letters patent and also with the surrendered reissues that preceded them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A chain of prior reissues and surrenders is relevant to identity analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary presumption of identity in reissued patents
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a legal presumption that the necessary identity of invention exists in all reissued patents; this presumption controls unless the contrary is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption may be rebutted only by introducing the original letters patent in evidence (or other contrary proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of essential original matter is fatal to identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Omitting from a reissue anything which the original specification stated to be essential to the invention is fatal to identity of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: omission of a single bolt from a reaper/mower reissue was enough to negative identity because with the bolt the machine was a reaper only. Also, a process is not the same as a machine that may perform it; a process of one stage is not the same as a multi‑stage process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original claimed multiple inventions — reissue may omit some
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an original patent described and claimed several different inventions, one or more of those inventions may be omitted from the claims of a reissue of that patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identity requires that the reissue claim no invention not described and intended to be claimed in the original, but the original may describe or claim inventions not present in the reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sub‑combination claiming in reissue (same function requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sub‑combination may be claimed in a reissue if it was shown in the original as performing the same function, even if it was claimed in the original only as part of a larger combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sub‑combination that is shown to perform a substantially different function in the reissue than it could perform in its original environment cannot be legally claimed in a reissue; the functional identity in original environment is decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate claim to a single device previously claimed only in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: A single device previously claimed only in combination may be made the subject of a separate claim in a reissue provided the device was a new and useful invention of the patentee, could have been separately claimed in the original, and appears in the original to have been intended to be secured thereby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits carving-out single elements when the original supports it by showing the element as an intended invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalents and scope broadening in reissue (Miller v. Brass rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a reissue may describe an equivalent of an original element and claim broadly enough to cover that equivalent depends on the application of Miller v. Brass Co.; such reissue may be sustained if applied for promptly after the original patent grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The right to obtain such a reissue is lost by long lapse of time after the date of the original and before the reissue application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal construction to preserve reissues (limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue patents are not to be held void for want of identity where a liberal construction of the original and reissue documents can avert that result; courts will modify claims by construction to make them conform to propriety where reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This remedial inclination cannot be relied on when a patent was surrendered and reissued solely to broaden its claim and the broadened claim is void for lack of novelty and identity. The claims of the reissued patent will be given their intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalid claims do not necessarily vitiate valid claims in same reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: If some, but not all, claims of a reissue patent are void (e.g., for violating Miller v. Brass or not being the same invention), that fact does not vitiate the other claims of that patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reissue will have whatever validity it would have had without the invalid claims, provided there is no unreasonable delay in filing an appropriate disclaimer of the invalid claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may apply/sign for reissue: executors/administrators/assignees
rubrics_metrics.description: Executors, administrators, or assignees have the same right to surrender and reissue a patent that the patentee has, subject to certain requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The application must be made and the new specification signed by the inventor himself if living and sane. Title to the reissued patent vests in an assignee by operation of assignment without a new document. A reissue granted to an administrator or executor is conclusive evidence of their authority; reissue to a trustee confers legal title on the trustee and equitable title on beneficiaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee vs grantee vs licensee definitions and joinder requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee receives the entire legal interest (or undivided part) in a patent by written instrument; a grantee's rights are confined to parts of U.S. territory; a licensee receives exclusive or concurrent rights to make/use/sell under the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reissue may be granted to an assignee of an assignee and such recitals make the reissued patent prima facie evidence of assignments. If a patent is owned jointly by multiple patentees or assignees, all owners must join in or ratify a reissue or it will be void; grantees and licensees are not required to join.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grantees' election between original and reissued patent rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Grantees may either continue to hold their rights under the original patent after it is surrendered and reissued by the patentee or may take corresponding rights under the reissued patent; they have a choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can theoretically lead to a single invention being patented in one part of the U.S. while free in another. In practice patentees/assignees seldom surrender claims worth retaining, and grantees often ratify broadened reissues. Statutory change could require all assignees/grantees to join in surrender to avoid such disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal effect of a valid reissued patent (dating and operation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent so reissued, together with the corrected specification, shall have the same effect and operation in law on actions thereafter arising as if the same had been originally filed in the corrected form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty for the reissued patent dates from the original invention/application; later developments after the original date cannot affect the reissued patent's novelty. However, when reissued patents are used as evidence against other patents, they operate as of their own reissue dates (not as of the original dates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for use/sale after reissue date
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who use or sell, after the date of a reissued patent, specimens of the thing covered by it are liable as infringers even if they made, bought, or used those specimens before that date when, due to omission from the original patent, they had a legal right to appropriate the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue thus can create liability for ongoing users who relied on incompleteness of the original patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional extensions — power and typical term
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may extend patents at any time (before or after expiration); such extensions are usually for seven years but lawfully may be for any limited length of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some special acts merely extend duration by edict; others instruct the Commissioner to ascertain facts and decide whether extension should be granted. Special acts are construed in connection with general patent laws and, as statutes, their validity generally cannot be collaterally attacked in court on grounds that passage was procured by fraud or bribery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office extensions — historical authorization and prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Office extensions were authorized by the Patent Act of July 4, 1836, but were prohibited by the Patent Act of March 3, 1861 as to patents thereafter granted; the last such extension was granted in 1875 and expired in 1882.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Patent Office extensions are historically limited, the legal doctrines developed in litigation over them are relevant to Congressional extensions and are explained in the treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for Patent Office extension applications (1836 scheme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Patent Act of 1836, a patentee desiring an extension might apply in writing to the Commissioner setting forth the grounds; on payment of a specified fee the Commissioner would publish notice of the application and when/where it would be considered; a board (Secretary of State, Commissioner of Patents, Solicitor of the Treasury) would hear and decide on the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes procedural prerequisites: written application stating grounds, fee, publication/notice, and administrative hearing before a multi‑member board; later special acts might change mode by instructing the Commissioner to investigate facts and make decisions in light of justice and public policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who might apply and who benefits from Patent Office extensions (headings/criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Heading‑level standards stated) Patent Office extension might be granted to an inventor‑patentee even if he had parted with all interest in the first term of his patent; extensions grantable only where inventors would possess, or at least participate in, the benefit thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are stated criteria in the table of contents indicating substantive limits on who may apply and equitable considerations (inventor's participation/benefit) though the chunk contains mainly the headings rather than full elaboration.
